opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the really interesting tensions in robotics right now. On one hand, we want these big, powerful models that understand the world semantically, can follow language instructions, and draw on all this web-scale knowledge. On the other hand, a robot arm needs commands at something like fifty or a hundred hertz, and you can't run a multi-billion-parameter model from scratch every few milliseconds.

The way I think about it is that people don't do that either. You don't deliberate consciously about every muscle twitch. There's a hierarchy. Some part of your brain is thinking slowly about what you're trying to accomplish, and much faster, more reactive processes handle the fine-grained motor control. A lot of what we've been doing reflects that structure.

One concrete version is action chunking. Instead of the model outputting one action per time step, it outputs a short trajectory, maybe half a second or a second of motion, and the robot executes that while the model is already thinking about the next chunk. In our pi-zero models, for example, there's an action expert that uses flow matching to produce a continuous chunk of actions, conditioned on the representations from the vision-language backbone. So the expensive reasoning is amortized over many control steps.

There are also ways to make this smoother, like real-time chunking, where the model generates the next chunk while the current one is executing and stays consistent with what's already committed. That way you don't get pauses or jerky transitions between chunks.

More broadly, I think we'll end up with systems that have a spectrum of timescales. At the top, something reasons about the task, maybe even in language: "Okay, I need to pick up the shirt first, then fold the sleeves." Below that, a policy turns those intentions into motion chunks. At the very bottom, low-level controllers handle the really high-frequency stuff, like impedance control and reacting to contact forces. The trick is training these together so the layers actually understand each other, rather than hand-engineering the interfaces like classical robotics did.

So the short answer is: don't do all the computation at every time step. Do the heavy thinking at a slower rate, let it produce something that covers a stretch of time, and leave the fast reactive part to lighter-weight machinery. That's very much how biological systems seem to work too.

r001.rationale: It says not to do all the computation at every time step and assigns fast reactive control to lighter-weight machinery.

r002.rationale: It describes planning and executing motion chunks, but does not state that advance planning sets initial conditions for a process that then unfolds during execution.

r003.rationale: It pairs planned motion chunks with low-level controllers that react to contact forces, communicating feedback at a more basic control level.

r004.rationale: It describes control layers at different timescales, but does not propose choosing representations based on whether they support advance planning or require a tight feedback loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a really interesting question, and I think the answer is that you don't need to do extensive computation at every time step, and in fact, biological systems don't do that either. If you look at how humans and animals control their bodies, there's a lot of hierarchy. You have very fast reflexive loops at the level of the spinal cord that are running at very high frequencies, and then you have slower, more deliberative processes running on top of that in the cortex, which are setting goals, setting intentions, and the fast loops are the ones that actually keep you from falling over when you step on something unexpected.

And I think with robots, we can do something very similar. So one way to think about it is that the thing that's computationally expensive, the big model, the thing that's doing the reasoning about the scene, understanding the task, figuring out what you're supposed to be doing, that doesn't need to run at a thousand hertz. It can run at a few hertz, or even slower. What it produces is something like a plan, or an intention, or a sequence of actions over the next second or so. And then you have a lower-level controller that takes that and executes it, and that lower-level controller can be very cheap, it can be a small network or even a classical controller that runs really fast and handles the local corrections.

The way we've been doing this in practice, with things like action chunking, is the model outputs a chunk of actions, say the next fifty time steps, and then the robot executes those while the next chunk is being computed. So the latency of the big model gets amortized over the whole chunk. And it turns out that works surprisingly well, because for most manipulation tasks the world doesn't change that much in a few hundred milliseconds. You're not playing ping pong, you're picking up a cup, and the cup is going to be in roughly the same place.

Now, where that breaks down is when you genuinely need fast reactive behavior, when something unexpected happens. And I think that's where the interesting research questions are. You want the fast loop to be smart enough to handle disturbances, but you don't want it to be so smart that it's expensive again. One thing we've looked at is having the big model not just output actions but output something more like a policy, or constraints on the policy, so the fast loop has more latitude to respond. Another thing is asynchronous inference, where you're always computing the next chunk while executing the current one, and you blend them, so you never actually have to wait.

But I think the broader point is that the premise that you need to do all your thinking at every time step is kind of a false constraint. The right structure is hierarchical, and once you accept that, the real-time problem becomes a lot more tractable.

r001.rationale: It says the fast lower-level controller can be cheap while running rapidly, and that the expensive model need not run at every time step.

r002.rationale: It describes planning and executing action chunks, but does not explain that advance movement planning sets initial conditions for a process that then unfolds during execution.

r003.rationale: It says the lower-level controller executes the planned actions and handles local corrections and disturbances, retaining feedback below the planner’s level.

r004.rationale: It contrasts action chunks for planned execution with policy-like outputs or constraints that give the fast loop room to respond.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you don’t need to solve the entire problem from scratch at every time step. You can do a lot of computation during training and amortize that into a policy—a neural network that maps observations to actions. Executing that policy can be much cheaper than doing the reasoning or optimization that produced it.

You can also have different processes operating at different timescales. If I’m reaching for a cup, I don’t need to reconsider why I want the cup every time I adjust my fingers. A slower process can decide what to do, while a faster controller handles the details and responds to feedback.

The important thing is that the fast controller still has to be competent. You can’t just make a plan and execute it blindly, because things move, contact is unpredictable, and your model is imperfect. But reacting to those changes doesn’t necessarily require extensive deliberation. That ability can be learned.

r001.rationale: It says policy execution is cheaper and that responding to changes does not require extensive deliberation at each step.

r002.rationale: It describes slower and faster processes, but does not say advance planning sets initial conditions for a process that unfolds during execution.

r003.rationale: It says a slower process decides what to do while a faster controller handles details and responds to feedback, as in adjusting fingers while reaching for a cup.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes processes by timescale, but does not propose choosing control representations based on support for advance planning versus a tight feedback loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t need to solve the entire problem from scratch at every time step. You can do a lot of the computation during training, and then distill the result into a policy that runs very quickly. The policy is essentially amortizing the work of figuring out what to do across all those training experiences.

You can also have different parts of the system operating at different frequencies. If you’re deciding which object to pick up, that decision doesn’t need to happen a thousand times a second. But the controller that adjusts the forces in your fingers might need to run much faster. So you can have a slower process doing more deliberative reasoning and a fast policy handling the immediate feedback.

The important thing is that the fast component can respond to what actually happens. You don’t want the robot to make a plan and then execute it blindly while it waits for the next round of reasoning. You want that learned controller continuously correcting its behavior based on what it sees and feels.

r001.rationale: The response says computation can be done during training and distilled into a policy that runs quickly, while a controller can operate much faster. This communicates that high-frequency control need not redo extensive computation at each step.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes slower decisions from faster control, but does not say advance movement planning sets initial conditions for a process that unfolds during execution.

r003.rationale: It says a fast controller corrects behavior using feedback, but does not state that this feedback operates at a more basic level of abstraction than the advance plan.

r004.rationale: The response describes components running at different frequencies, but does not propose choosing control representations based on their suitability for advance planning versus tight feedback.
